attractions.note: from column: Kurama: A Hidden Mountain Retreat in Kyoto’s Wilderness (heading: Kuramadera: Kyoto’s Sacred Mountain Temple)

attractions.description_en: Source: Japan Guide

attractions.description_en: We started our trip with a drive to Shikanoshima Island , about 40 minutes from downtown Fukuoka. The island is surrounded by clear blue sea and low hills, making it a nice break from the city.
attractions.note: from column: 2 Days in Fukuoka: A Complete Itinerary of What to See, Do, and Eat (heading: Morning: Shikanoshima Island)

attractions.description_en: Next, we made our way to Shikaumi Shrine , known as the main shrine for sea deities. The area is peaceful, and from the shrine grounds, you get a great view of the Genkai Sea. It’s a popular spot among locals, who come here to pray for safety and prosperity.
attractions.note: from column: 2 Days in Fukuoka: A Complete Itinerary of What to See, Do, and Eat (heading: Late Morning: Shikaumi Shrine)

attractions.description_en: Located at the entrance of the island, The Luigans Spa & Resort was where we stopped for lunch and a short break. The open layout, ocean views, and poolside area make it feel like a relaxing getaway, even though it’s still so close to the city. If you have time, it’s a nice spot to unwind, especiall
attractions.note: from column: 2 Days in Fukuoka: A Complete Itinerary of What to See, Do, and Eat (heading: Afternoon: The Luigans Spa & Resort)

attractions.description_en: We started our second day at Hakata Old Town , one of Fukuoka’s oldest districts known for its shrines, traditional shops, and preserved buildings. Our first stop was Kushida Shrine , one of the city’s most well-known shrines and the main site of the Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival (a summer event whe
attractions.note: from column: 2 Days in Fukuoka: A Complete Itinerary of What to See, Do, and Eat (heading: Morning: Hakata Old Town)

attractions.description_en: In the afternoon, we joined a Hakata River Cruise , which offered a different view of the city. Seeing Fukuoka from the water, passing under bridges and alongside the city’s buildings, was relaxing and surprisingly scenic. At night, the reflections of neon signs and food stall lanterns on the river
attractions.note: from column: 2 Days in Fukuoka: A Complete Itinerary of What to See, Do, and Eat (heading: Afternoon: Hakata River Cruise)

attractions.description_en: We wrapped up our day at the yatai food stalls , one of Fukuoka’s most famous local experiences. Yatai are small open-air food stalls that pop up along the streets in the evening, each serving simple dishes such as ramen, yakitori, and oden. They are especially popular near the Nakasu river , where
attractions.note: from column: 2 Days in Fukuoka: A Complete Itinerary of What to See, Do, and Eat (heading: Evening: Yatai Food Stalls)

attractions.description_en: Nagoya Castle is one of the city’s most recognisable landmarks and an important symbol of Aichi’s history. Originally built in the early 17th century by Tokugawa Ieyasu, the castle served as a key defensive base during the Edo period. Its most famous feature is the pair of golden shachihoko roof orn
attractions.note: from column: Discovering the Charm of the Chita Peninsula: 6 Places to Explore Near Nagoya (heading: Nagoya Castle)

attractions.description_en: Osu Shopping Street is located a short distance from Nagoya Castle and offers a different side of the city. This traditional shopping street features a wide mix of shops, including vintage clothing stores, souvenir shops and street snack stalls.
attractions.note: from column: Discovering the Charm of the Chita Peninsula: 6 Places to Explore Near Nagoya (heading: Osu Shopping Street)

attractions.description_en: Ghibli Park is a must-visit attraction for fans of Studio Ghibli. Located within Expo 2005 Aichi Commemorative Park, just outside Nagoya, the park recreates the worlds of beloved films such as My Neighbour Totoro, Spirited Away and Howl’s Moving Castle.
attractions.note: from column: Discovering the Charm of the Chita Peninsula: 6 Places to Explore Near Nagoya (heading: Ghibli Park)

attractions.description_en: Source: Japan Guide
attractions.note: from column: Discovering the Charm of the Chita Peninsula: 6 Places to Explore Near Nagoya (heading: Meiji Village)

attractions.description_en: Another place worth adding to your itinerary is Atsuta Jingu Shrine. With a history of more than 1,900 years, it is one of the most important Shinto shrines (traditional Japanese religion shrine) in Japan.
attractions.note: from column: Why Nagoya, Japan Is Worth Exploring: Must-Visit Places and Local Food to Try (heading: Atsuta Jingu Shrine)

attractions.description_en: Having taken a look into Japan’s samurai past, it is time to dive into the world of traditional performing arts at Nagoya Noh Theatre. Designed in an elegant Japanese architectural style, the venue is home to one of the largest indoor Noh stages in Japan.
attractions.note: from column: Why Nagoya, Japan Is Worth Exploring: Must-Visit Places and Local Food to Try (heading: Nagoya Noh Theater)

attractions.description_en: Of course, exploring local shopping streets is part of the experience when you are in Japan. Head over to Endoji Shopping Street, Nagoya’s oldest shopping street that dates all the way back to the Edo period (1603-1868). Tucked away near the historic Shikemichi district, this charming place offers a
attractions.note: from column: Why Nagoya, Japan Is Worth Exploring: Must-Visit Places and Local Food to Try (heading: Endoji Shopping Street)

attractions.description_en: Marvel at the story behind one of Japan’s leading companies at the Toyota Commemorative Museum of Industry and Technology. Located in a red-brick factory building from the Taisho era, the museum stands in the very place where the Toyota Group’s story first began.
attractions.note: from column: Why Nagoya, Japan Is Worth Exploring: Must-Visit Places and Local Food to Try (heading: Toyota Commemorative Museum of Industry and Technology)

attractions.description_en: After riding Japan’s famous Shinkansen (Japanese bullet train), why not learn more about the technology behind it at SCMAGLEV and Railway Park? The museum showcases the development of trains in Japan, from nostalgic steam locomotives to futuristic superconducting maglev trains (high-speed trains usi
attractions.note: from column: Why Nagoya, Japan Is Worth Exploring: Must-Visit Places and Local Food to Try (heading: SCMAGLEV and Railway Park)

attractions.description_en: Nagoya’s innovation goes beyond trains and cars. If you enjoy cooking or simply love food, make a stop at Vermicular Village, the birthplace of the well-known Vermicular cast iron enamel pot developed by a long-established manufacturer in Aichi Prefecture.
attractions.note: from column: Why Nagoya, Japan Is Worth Exploring: Must-Visit Places and Local Food to Try (heading: Vermicular Village)

attractions.description_en: While takoyaki is commonly associated with Osaka, Nagoya offers its own take on this popular street snack. A local twist on the classic, Nagoya-style takoyaki is seasoned with soy sauce instead of the usual sweet sauce and mayonnaise. The soy sauce is added directly to the batter as it cooks, giving
attractions.note: from column: Why Nagoya, Japan Is Worth Exploring: Must-Visit Places and Local Food to Try (heading: Soy Sauce Takoyaki)

attractions.description_en: Miso katsu is one of Nagoya’s signature local dishes. It features a deep-fried pork cutlet coated in crispy panko breadcrumbs, served with a rich sauce made from fermented soybean paste known as miso. The pork cutlet is crunchy on the outside and tender on the inside, while the thick miso sauce adds
attractions.note: from column: Why Nagoya, Japan Is Worth Exploring: Must-Visit Places and Local Food to Try (heading: Miso Katsu)

attractions.description_en: Hitsumabushi is a Nagoya specialty made with grilled eel served over a bowl of rice. The eel is charcoal-grilled until slightly crispy on the outside and brushed with a savoury-sweet soy-based sauce that gives it a rich flavour. What makes this dish unique is the way it is enjoyed in several steps.
attractions.note: from column: Why Nagoya, Japan Is Worth Exploring: Must-Visit Places and Local Food to Try (heading: Hitsumabushi)

attractions.description_en: Tebasaki are Nagoya-style chicken wings known for their crispy texture and bold seasoning. The wings are deep-fried without batter, then coated in a savoury-sweet sauce made with soy sauce, garlic, and sugar, and finished with a generous sprinkle of black pepper. Unlike typical fried chicken, tebasa
attractions.note: from column: Why Nagoya, Japan Is Worth Exploring: Must-Visit Places and Local Food to Try (heading: Tebasaki)

attractions.description_en: We started our day at Tsurugaoka Hachimangu, a well-known shrine in Kamakura. It is dedicated to Hachiman, a deity closely linked to the Minamoto clan and the samurai era.
attractions.note: from column: Places to Visit in Kamakura for a Day Trip (heading: Tsurugaoka Hachimangu)

attractions.description_en: A short distance away, we visited Hasedera Temple. We learned that it is often called the “Temple of Flowers” because the hillside is planted with different flowers that change with the seasons. Sadly, we didn’t get to see them in full bloom during our visit, but we heard that it looks especially be
attractions.note: from column: Places to Visit in Kamakura for a Day Trip (heading: Hasedera Temple)

attractions.description_en: Next, we stopped by Engakuji Temple, one of the main Zen temples in Kamakura. As we walked in, the first thing we noticed was the large Sanmon Gate.
attractions.note: from column: Places to Visit in Kamakura for a Day Trip (heading: Engakuji Temple)

attractions.description_en: This was the last temple we visited, Hokokuji Temple, which is also known as the Bamboo Temple. It felt quite different from the others because of its famous bamboo grove.
attractions.note: from column: Places to Visit in Kamakura for a Day Trip (heading: Hokokuji Temple)

attractions.description_en: No visit to Kamakura is complete without trying the local food. We visited Komachi-dori Street, a popular shopping street located near Kamakura Station.
attractions.note: from column: Places to Visit in Kamakura for a Day Trip (heading: Komachi-dori Street)

attractions.description_en: Mount Yoshinoyama is one of the main highlights for cherry blossom viewing in Yoshino. It is famous for Senbonzakura , referring to the thousands of cherry trees found across the area. Today, more than 30,000 trees can be seen across the mountain, creating layers of blossoms that gradually appear as
attractions.note: from column: Where to Go in Yoshino, Nara for Sakura Views (heading: Mount Yoshinoyama)

attractions.description_en: One notable spot here is the Ishibutai Tumulus, located within Asuka Historical National Government Park, which is a popular place to see cherry blossoms. In spring, the cherry trees bloom around one of Japan’s largest stone burial chambers, adding a seasonal burst of colour around the massive stone

attractions.description_en: Of course, the main reason I visited Akabeko Land was to paint my own akabeko. I visited the Iimoriyama store, where you can learn more about the folk toy before creating your own. There are also games and photo spots around the facility to check out before or after your painting session.
attractions.note: from column: Experience 3 Eras in 1 Day: A Guide to Aizu, Fukushima (heading: Paint Your Own Akabeko)

attractions.description_en: Founded in 2015 , Akiu Winery holds the distinction of being the first winery established in Miyagi Prefecture after the Great East Japan Earthquake. Not simply a producer of wine, it was created with the vision of revitalising the community, supporting regional agriculture, and celebrating the flav
attractions.note: from column: Akiu Winery: A Taste of Miyagi’s Countryside in Every Glass (heading: Akiu Winery at a Glance)

attractions.description_en: One of the most well-known landmarks in Kumamoto, Kumamoto Castle is widely regarded as one of Japan’s most impressive castles for its striking defensive design and historical significance. Built in the early 1600s by feudal lord Kato Kiyomasa, the castle became known as one of Japan’s strongest for
attractions.note: from column: Discover The Best Of Kumamoto: From Aso To Kurokawa Onsen In Kyushu (heading: Exploring Kumamoto Castle)

attractions.description_en: Another way to experience Aso’s connection to nature and agriculture is by visiting Aso Milk Farm, a dairy farm surrounded by the region’s natural volcanic landscapes. Located along the outer rim of Mount Aso at an altitude of around 430 metres, the farm overlooks the surrounding countryside and mou
attractions.note: from column: Discover The Best Of Kumamoto: From Aso To Kurokawa Onsen In Kyushu (heading: Spend The Day At Rakunoh Mother’s Aso Milk Farm)

attractions.description_en: Takayama’s Old Town is one of Hida Takayama’s most popular areas. Here, timber-framed merchant houses from the Edo period line the streets, creating one of the most atmospheric townscapes in Gifu. Long-established sake breweries, craft shops, cafes, and family-run businesses continue welcoming visit
attractions.note: from column: Your Travel Guide to Gifu Prefecture: Gero Onsen, Hida Takayama and Shirakawa-go (heading: Takayama’s Old Town: A Living Edo-Period Town)

attractions.description_en: To experience a different side of local life, start your morning at the Miyagawa Morning Market. Held daily along the banks of the Miyagawa River, this busy market has a history dating back more than a century and remains one of Japan’s most famous morning markets.
attractions.note: from column: Your Travel Guide to Gifu Prefecture: Gero Onsen, Hida Takayama and Shirakawa-go (heading: Experience Local Life at the Miyagawa Morning Market)

attractions.description_en: Among the different modes of transport along the Alpine Route, the Tateyama Ropeway was one of our favourites. Often described as a moving observation deck, the ropeway connects Daikanbo and Kurobedaira in just seven minutes while offering uninterrupted panoramic views of the surrounding mountains.
attractions.note: from column: Why the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route Should Be on Your Japan Bucket List (heading: Taking in the Views on the Tateyama Ropeway)

attractions.description_en: At the foot of Mount Yufu lies Yufuin Onsen, one of Japan’s most celebrated hot spring destinations. Surrounded by rolling mountains and lush countryside, the town has long attracted visitors seeking a peaceful retreat where nature, traditional ryokan, and therapeutic hot springs come together.
attractions.note: from column: Things to Do in Oita: Experience Japan's Finest Hot Springs and Local Cuisine (heading: Yufuin Onsen: A Hot Spring Town Shaped by Nature)

attractions.description_en: No visit to Yufuin is complete without stopping by Lake Kinrin, one of the town’s most well-known landmarks. Surrounded by verdant greenery at the foot of Mount Yufu, the lake offers a peaceful escape where visitors can slow down and immerse themselves in the tranquil natural scenery.
attractions.note: from column: Things to Do in Oita: Experience Japan's Finest Hot Springs and Local Cuisine (heading: Lake Kinrin: Yufuin’s Most Enchanting Morning View)

attractions.description_en: After experiencing the quieter side of Yufuin, it’s time to discover a completely different side of Oita in Beppu, a city renowned for its impressive geothermal landscape and rich hot spring culture. Unlike Yufuin’s tranquil countryside, Beppu is instantly recognisable by the clouds of steam rising
attractions.note: from column: Things to Do in Oita: Experience Japan's Finest Hot Springs and Local Cuisine (heading: Beppu Onsen: Japan’s Famous Hot Spring City)
